newsitem.title: USA: Muted demand seen for US index-linked bond launch.
newsitem.headline: Muted demand seen for US index-linked bond launch.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury's inaugural index-linked bond auction is not expected to be a disaster, but players forsee limited demand for the new notes.

On Wednesday, Treasury is slated to sell $7 billion of the inflation protected 10-year notes. In when-issued trading Monday, the notes were yielding 3.50 percent, after the yield fell as low as 3.30 percent last week.
Traders said 3.50 percent to 3.75 percent is fair value for the 10-year notes, but they doubted investors would jump at the low end of that range.

"I really haven't seen people knocking down the door and buying them," said Neil DeSarno, head government bond trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. "Everyone is nibbling and thinking about it, but I don't see a lot of committment."
Part of the problem, some traders and portfolio managers said, was that they did not fully understand the new notes.

As such, since the auction's announcement last week, trading volume has been fairly weak, with only about $100 million to $200 million a day -- or about $1.5 billion total -- traded in the issue, traders said.

Underscoring the nervousness over the index-linked bonds was a recent survey by Reid Thunberg & Co. Of the 64 investment managers, controlling more than $400 million in fixed income assets, 88 percent said they do not plan to buy the new notes.
Among the reasons cited included: the notes do not fit into portfolios; they are "untested;" the 10-year maturity is too long; and mistrust of the consumer price index.
One 10-year trader at a leading U.S. primary dealership said he was surprised at the survey results.
"Trading volume has been disappointing but I don't think it will be the disaster (the survey) paints," the trader said.
Other traders said they would snatch up some of the new notes despite the market's less-than-enthusiastic sentiment toward the Treasury's new financing plan.

"We are going to try and buy some," said Scott Graham, a government bond trader at Prudential Securities Inc. "We think we can make money on them the next three, four months. People are going to be rewarded for buying them ... Eventually they will settle at 3.35, 3.40 percent."

Graham added that he thought it would take some cheapening up for the Street to take down all $7 billion. He said he thought it was possible that slack demand could push the issue's yield to 3.60 percent to 3.70 percent.
"They are clearly worth taking a shot at," Graham said, adding that insurance companies and some money managers should gobble them up.
Market participants noted that there is seemingly little difference between the index-linked 10-year note and regular 10-year note.

At 6.67 percent, the regular 10-year note yield is only slightly above its index-linked counterpart -- yielding 3.5 percent plus about a 3.0 percent rate of expected inflation in 1997, totalling 6.50 percent.

"No one can say for sure how the indexed linked bonds will perform relative to conventional Treasuries," said Nanette Abuhoff, senior fixed income strategist at J.P. Morgan & Co. (( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
